summary:
FlameScope is a web app that turns decades of NASA microgravity fire research into a fire-risk tool for future Moon and Mars habitats. Users set cabin conditions (oxygen, pressure, airflow and gravity), choose materials, and see which ones would burn, ranked by how far the cabin's oxygen is above each material's flammability limit, with the NASA test behind every result.

We collected 81 NASA sources: NTRS papers, PSI investigations (BASS, Saffire, FLEX) and NASA pages on Apollo 1, Mir and FM2. An AI model reads them and extracts test conditions; Python then checks that every number appears in a real source sentence, so the rankings are traceable math, not AI guesses. FlameScope also answers questions with citations and maps knowledge gaps, such as the lack of tests at lunar or Martian gravity.

This addresses the challenge by summarizing, ranking and interpreting NASA's fire research. It matters because NASA's planned exploration atmosphere (34% oxygen at 8.2 psia) can make materials that are safe on the ISS flammable: in our demo, Nomex goes from "no data" to "burns".
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FlameScope is a fire-risk tool for future Moon and Mars habitats, built from NASA's own microgravity combustion research. You set your habitat's air (oxygen %, pressure, airflow and gravity) or pick a preset (ISS cabin, Lunar habitat, Mars habitat, Earth lab), choose cabin materials, and FlameScope ranks them by fire risk. Every result links to the NASA test it came from.

It has four parts:

- Risk ranking: for each material, the gap between the cabin's oxygen level and the lowest oxygen level at which that material has been shown to burn. Tests run in conditions closer to yours count more.

- Evidence explorer: charts that place your cabin among real NASA test results.

- Ask the archive: answers questions using only NASA passages, with numbered citations.

- Knowledge gaps: shows which materials NASA has never tested at lunar or Martian gravity or at high oxygen.

HOW IT WORKS

We collected 81 NASA sources: 40 NASA Technical Reports Server papers, 26 Physical Sciences Informatics investigations (BASS, Saffire, FLEX and others), 3 PSI documents, and NASA pages on Apollo 1, Apollo 13, the Mir fire and the FM2, SoFIE and FLARE experiments. They were split into 1,509 searchable passages. An AI model reads the papers and copies out test conditions (material, oxygen, pressure, flow, gravity, outcome). Python then converts the units, removes impossible values, and keeps a row only if its numbers appear together in a real sentence from the paper. Of 79 extracted rows, 20 passed this check, and only those feed the ranking. The AI never produces a ranking; the ranking is simple, traceable math.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

NASA's planned exploration atmosphere (34% oxygen at 8.2 psia) can make materials that are acceptable on the ISS flammable. In our demo, Nomex has no burn data at ISS conditions, but in the lunar habitat preset it sits at least 11 percentage points above its oxygen limit. FlameScope gives habitat designers, students and researchers a fast way to see this, check the evidence, and spot where new tests are needed.

TOOLS

Python 3.12, Streamlit, pandas, Plotly, PyMuPDF, rank-bm25 (search), BeautifulSoup and requests. A free local AI model (Qwen2.5 3B via Ollama) runs on an ordinary laptop CPU with no GPU, no API key and no cost. The NASA NTRS and PSI public APIs supply the data. The public version runs entirely in the visitor's browser (stlite/Pyodide), hosted on Cloudflare Workers from GitHub.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It turns decades of scattered papers into one structured, checkable dataset. It shows its own blind spots instead of guessing: where no test exists at lunar or Martian gravity, it says so. And it needs no server or sign-up; anyone with a link can use it.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Trust (no AI-invented numbers, and every claim is cited), safety (missing data is shown as missing, never as "safe"), zero cost, low-end hardware, and accessibility for non-specialists.

USE OF AI

We used Anthropic's Claude as a coding, debugging and writing assistant, and the local Qwen2.5 model inside the app to extract test data and write cited answers. All extracted numbers are checked against the source text by code.
